prompt.context: Your client is a shoe and clothing manufacturer ('Dering Co.') that has over $500MM in sales. Dering Co. has been successful in its traditional market for apparel and men's casual dress shoes, but growth is slowing in this market and margins are declining. The company is U.S. based, but has a manufacturing facility in a low-cost SE Asian country. Several board members, who have backgrounds in the athletic shoe industry, believe that your client should, broadly speaking, enter the athletic shoe market. The athletic shoe market in total is $20 billion today.
prompt.question: How would you think about this athletic shoe opportunity?

clarifying_info.q: What is the growth rate — is it annual or total?
clarifying_info.a: Growth is total growth (not annual or compound annual growth rate) projected over the next 5 years.

clarifying_info.q: What time horizon do the margin figures apply to?
clarifying_info.a: Margins are projected EBIT margins in 5 years.

clarifying_info.q: What is included in the 'Other' category in the market share data?
clarifying_info.a: Wilson controls 45% to 50% of the Court market (contained in the Other category). In all other segments, Other contains players with very small market shares.

exhibits.title: Market Size Statistics
exhibits.shows: A table of the overall athletic footwear market ($20 billion today) broken into 6 segments, showing each segment's percentage of total revenue, projected 5-year growth rate, and projected EBIT margin in 5 years.

exhibits.title: Market Share by Segment
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart showing relative market share (%) for Nike, Adidas, Reebok, and Other across the six athletic footwear segments: Basketball, Running, Cross Training, Walking/Fashion, Court, and Soccer.

framework: Assess market attractiveness by segment: size, growth, and profit pool
Evaluate competitive intensity and fragmentation by segment
Overlay Dering Co.'s internal capabilities and existing business fit
Synthesize to recommend the most attractive entry segment(s)
Identify risks, distribution channel considerations, and next steps

questions.prompt: Question 1: Using Exhibit 1, which segments are most attractive and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate projected future revenue for each segment (current revenue × (1 + growth%)), then multiply by projected EBIT margin to get the absolute profit pool. Rankings should be based on profit pool size, NOT on margin % alone or on revenue size alone. Top three segments by profit pool: Running ($1.2B), Court ($1.125B), Walking/Fashion ($0.9B). Cross Training and Basketball are mid-tier; Soccer is least attractive on profit pool despite highest margin %.

math.setup: Current market = $20B. Segment current revenue = $20B × %Rev. Projected revenue = current revenue × (1 + growth%). Profit pool = projected revenue × EBIT margin.
steps: Total projected market: $30.7B; Total profit pool: $5.155B; Blended margin: ~17%; Revenue CAGR: ~8.9%
math.answer: Profit pool ranking: 1st Running ($1.200B), 2nd Court ($1.125B), 3rd Walking/Fashion ($0.900B), 4th Basketball ($0.800B), 5th Cross Training ($0.650B), 6th Soccer ($0.480B).

questions.prompt: Question 2: Using Exhibit 2, which segments are most attractive from a competitive/fragmentation standpoint?
questions.guidance: Fragmented markets (lower share concentration) are more attractive for a new entrant. Candidate should read market share bars and assess concentration. Fragmentation ranking most-to-least attractive: Court (appears very fragmented with 68% Other — but candidate should ask what 'Other' contains), Walking/Fashion, Cross Training, Running, Basketball, Soccer. Critical insight: when asked about 'Other' in Court, Wilson controls 45-50% of Court — so Court is actually less fragmented than it appears. Combining profit pool rank and fragmentation rank: Walking/Fashion ranks 2nd on fragmentation and 3rd on profit pool, making it the best combined opportunity. Court drops significantly once Wilson's dominance is revealed.

math.setup: No calculation required; qualitative assessment of market share concentration.
steps: Fragmentation rank (unadjusted): Court (1st), Walk/Fashion (2nd), Cross (3rd), Run (4th), Basketball (5th), Soccer (6th)
After Wilson reveal: Court becomes less attractive — Wilson controls ~45-50% of Court
Combined profit pool + fragmentation ranking: Walking/Fashion and Running emerge as top targets
math.answer: Walking/Fashion is most attractive on combined basis. Court initially appears attractive but Wilson's dominance in 'Other' makes it concentrated. Soccer ranks last on both dimensions.

questions.prompt: Question 3: Given the additional qualitative information about each segment, what is your final conclusion?
questions.guidance: Candidate should synthesize qualitative context with quantitative findings. Key points by segment: Basketball — low EBIT margins due to high sales/marketing and branding costs; Running — high price points but the high-end (60%) requires significant R&D/technology, low-end (40%) may be more accessible and fits casual/fashion positioning; Cross Training — no distinctive insight; Walking/Fashion — fashion-conscious consumers with likely overlap with Dering Co.'s core apparel customer base and distribution; Court — controlled by Wilson through specialty retail, difficult for new entrant; Soccer — 75% sold through specialty soccer-only stores, challenging distribution. Conclusion: Walking/Fashion is the recommended entry segment. Strong overlap with core apparel customers, fragmented competition, solid profit pool ($900M), no need for specialized R&D, and compatible distribution channels.

brainstorming.prompt: What additional information would you want before making a final recommendation on market entry?

categories.name: Internal capabilities
ideas: Dering Co.'s existing design/fashion expertise applicable to walking/fashion segment
Manufacturing capabilities in SE Asia for athletic footwear vs. casual shoes
Current distribution channels and retailer relationships
Brand perception and strength in target customer segment

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: Detailed breakdown of 'Other' in each segment
Wilson's competitive moat in Court segment
Barriers to entry in Running high-end (R&D, patents, technology)
Pricing power and brand loyalty in each segment

categories.name: Customer and channel
ideas: Overlap between Dering Co.'s current apparel customers and walking/fashion shoe buyers
Channel mix — general retail vs. specialty stores for each segment
Consumer willingness to pay for a new brand

categories.name: Financial
ideas: Required investment to enter (branding, tooling, R&D by segment)
Time to profitability and payback period
Margin potential for Dering Co. specifically given its cost structure

recommendation: Enter the Walking/Fashion athletic footwear segment as the primary recommendation: $900M profit pool (3rd largest), 20% projected EBIT margin, most fragmented competition among attractive segments (after adjusting for Wilson in Court), and strong strategic fit with Dering Co.'s existing apparel/fashion customer base and distribution channels.

Conduct further diligence on the low-end of the Running segment (40% of the market) as a secondary opportunity, given its larger profit pool ($480M of the $1.2B total, roughly), more accessible price points, and potential fashion/casual positioning consistent with Dering Co.'s brand.
risks: Walking/Fashion segment may require brand investment to compete with established players
Running low-end may have lower margins than the blended 20% figure if high-end skews margins up
New entrant without athletic heritage may face consumer credibility challenges
SE Asian manufacturing facility may require retooling for athletic footwear construction
next_steps: Validate margin structure specifically for Walking/Fashion sub-segment
Assess distribution channel access — confirm existing retail relationships cover this category
Evaluate brand strategy: launch under Dering Co. brand vs. create new sub-brand
Size required capex for product development, tooling, and go-to-market
